2 Introduction The objective of this research is to characterize the population structure and prevalence of copper resistance of the walnut blight pathogen, Xanthomonas arboricola pv. juglandis ( Xaj ) collected in central and Northern California between the years of 1994 to 2019. Additionally, we are interested in elucidating the type III secretion system effector (T3E) diversity and assessing where the Californian Xaj population fits in a global context. We also sequenced 20 strains of Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni ( Xap ), the causal agent of bacterial spot of almond, and included those in some of the analyses. 2.1 Hypotheses Genes associated with and/or responsible for copper resistance are prevalent in the CA Xanthomonas arboricola pv. juglandis population and correlate with the respective copper-sensitivity phenotype in vitro. Xaj and Xap exhibit variation in type III secretion system effector repertoires. CA Xaj strains form distinct genetic clusters when compared with other global strains. The CA Xaj population does not encode any plasmids.

3 Methods 3.1 Read Processing Whole-genome sequencing from Novogene generated high-quality reads (Table 4.1). Novogene provides reads that have been filtered based on the following criteria: Remove reads containing adapters. Remove reads containing N > 10% (N represents the base cannot be determined). Remove reads containing low quality (Qscore<= 5) base which is over 50% of the total base. However, I performed an additional filtering step using FastP v0.23.4 (Chen et al. (2018)). The filters I’m applying are as follows: -q 30 (the quality value that a base is qualified) --detect_adapter_for_pe (automatically detect adapter sequence based on paired end reads, and remove them) Since we received ~2x the amount of sequencing data than we were quoted for, I chose to filter the data for the highest quality reads (q \(\geq 30\)). I also opted to enable the auto-detection for adapter removal. Novogene removes most adapter sequences but < 1% of the read sets contain adapter sequences so FastP should detect and remove the remainders. Please refer to FastP.sh (5.1.1) for the script. 3.2 Genome Assembly and Annotation Prior to settling on the pipeline detailed below, I tested several other pipelines that are detailed in XAJ_XAP_Project.v1.md, AS_Progress_Report_090924.v3.pptx, and Assembly_Pipeline_102424.pptx. Based on the findings from the pipeline tests, we settled on the following steps for de novo genome assembly and annotation (3.1): De novo assembly using Platanus_B v1.3.2 (Kajitani et al. (2020)). Generate assembly stats via QUAST v5.1.0rc1 (Gurevich et al. (2013)). Scaffold contigs using Ragout v2.3 (Kolmogorov et al. (2014)). Xaj isolate IVIA 1317 (NCBI Accession: GCF_023375035.1) (Cuesta-Morrondo et al. (2022)) was used as the reference for the Xaj population. Xap isolate 15-088 (NCBI Accession: GCF_008761555.1) was used as the reference for the Xap population. Polish scaffolds with Pilon (Walker et al. (2014)). Assess completeness and contamination with CheckM (Parks et al. (2015)). Annotate with NCBI PGAP (Tatusova et al. (2016)). Since I already generated the Bioproject and Biosamples I was able to generate NCBI-submission ready annotations. These are currently being processed by NCBI. Two samples had an error and I’m in communication with NCBI on how to resolve these errors. Figure 3.1: Xaj and Xap assembly pipeline 3.2.1 Steps 1-2. Platanus_B & QUAST I generated Assembly_Workflow_Platanus_B.csv and used it as my $SAMPFILE variable for running Platanus_B with the Step1.Assemble.sh (5.2.1) script. It contains 5 columns that detail the sample ID, Strain, filtered Read1, filtered Read2, and organism. The Assembly_Workflow_Platanus_B.csv file was converted to unix format using the dos2unix Assembly_Workflow_Platanus_B.csv command on the cluster and afterwards the nano Assembly_Workflow_Platanus_B.csv command was used to add one blank line at the end. Step1.Assemble.sh (5.2.1) generated the de novo assemblies (contigs) and QUAST was used to generate assembly statistics. I wrote a series of scripts to summarize the annotation and assembly results. These scripts are: Summarize_ANI.sh (5.2.2), Summarize_CheckM.sh (5.2.3), and Summarize_Genbank.py (5.2.4) 3.2.2 Step 3. Scaffolding Ragout v2.3 was used to scaffold the assemblies using Step2.Scaffold.sh (5.2.6) . I used Xaj 417 and IVIA 1317 as reference strains for Xaj and 15-088 as the reference strain for Xap. As mentioned previously, we opted to proceed with the Ragout scaffolds using the IVIA 1317 reference since it gave better results (see Assembly_Pipeline_102424.pptx). QUAST was also used to generate statistics for comparisons. Ragout uses .rcp files as inputs to set specific variables. I generated two template .rcp files for Xaj (XAJ_Template.rcp) and Xap (XAP_Template.rcp), respectively. These template files served as an input for .rcp file generation for each strain. XAJ_Strains.RCP.csv and XAP_Strains.RCP.csv served as input files for generating the .rcp files using Generate_RCP.sh (5.2.5). 3.2.3 Step 4. Polishing with Pilon Based on the the previous findings (see Assembly_Pipeline_102424.pptx), Pilon increased assembly quality. Pilon v1.24 using default settings were applied to the Ragout assemblies using Step3.Polish.sh (5.2.7). I used BWA-mem2 v2.2.1 (Vasimuddin et al. (2019)), and samtools v1.19.2 (Li et al. (2009)) prior to Pilon. These Pilon polished assemblies were used for the PGAP annotations. The Pilon-polished assemblies were then subjected to CheckM (Parks et al. (2015)) using the taxonomy option with Xanthomonas as the reference genus to assess completeness and contamination (see Step3.CheckM.sh (5.2.8)). 3.2.4 Step 5. Annotation I downloaded PGAP v2024-07-18.build7555 on my local computer because I was running into issues trying to install it on the cluster. Since these assemblies and annotations will be submitted to NCBI, I needed to generate $STRAIN.generic.yaml and $STRAIN.submol.yaml as inputs for PGAP to ensure that all metadata is correctly assigned. I wrote Generate_Generic_YAML.sh (5.2.9) and Generate_Submol_YAML.sh (5.2.10) to efficiently generate the .yaml files. The metadata was stored in Reference_Data_For_YAML.txt and each of the .yaml scripts used that file to generate the respective .yaml files. Next I wrote PGAP.sh (5.2.11), the core PGAP command, to generate the annotations and I called that script using Step4.Annotate.sh (5.2.12) because I was running this locally. 3.2.5 NCBI Submission Before we publish the manuscript we must submit our data (raw Illumina reads & annotated assemblies) to NCBI. I submitted all the raw reads from Novogene to the SRA under the BioProject PRJNA1151720 (3.1). The SRA submission has already been processed and will be released upon publication. The genomes are currently being processed as of January 17,2025. Unfortunately, XAJ2128 and XAJ934 had one error each that I must address before submission. The error is the same for both: [SEQ_FEAT.FeatureBeginsOrEndsInGap] Feature begins or ends in gap and only occurs for one gene (transposase) in each strain, respectively. Specifically, the beginning of the genes start with an ‘N’, but the respective protein started with an ‘M’. According to NCBI, the fix is to either remove the gene entirely or label the gene as ‘partial’. Since I’ve already performed genomic analyses (phylogeny, pangenome, etc.) I do not want to remove the gene. I emailed NCBI on January 21, 2025 to ask for assistance to make these changes to indicate that the transposase is indicated as ‘partial’. I’m confident that they will be able to help me make these changes. This is likely due to me using the --ignore-all-errors argument in PGAP.sh (5.2.11). I had to use that argument in order to make the program run.. otherwise the annotations would fail. It’s fine as the other annotations are processing just fine. To determine if the data is ‘clock-like’ you must detect a significant temporal signal by performing a root-to-tip regression analysis. “A data set is considered to have temporal signal if it can be treated as a measurably evolving population, defined by Drummond et al. (2003) as “populations from which molecular sequences can be taken at different points in time, among which there are a statistically significant number of genetic differences. (Duchene et al. (2020))” If there is a weak temporal signal, then the data does not exhibit clock-like behavior and is unfit for molecular dating analysis. I used two programs to detect temporal signal: TempEST v1.5.3 (Rambaut et al. (2016)) TempEst (short for “Temporal Explorer of Sequence Trees,” formerly known as Path-O-Gen) is a tool designed for analyzing the temporal signal and “clocklikeness” of molecular phylogenies. It’s widely used in evolutionary biology to assess whether a dataset of genetic sequences (e.g., from viruses or bacteria) shows a measurable rate of evolution over time. TempEst can handle both contemporaneous trees (all sequences collected at the same time) and dated-tip trees (sequences collected at different times). It helps researchers visualize the relationship between genetic divergence and sampling dates through root-to-tip regression plots, and it can suggest an optimal root for the tree that aligns with a molecular clock assumption. Since TempEST is a stand-alone software package with a GUI, I do not have any associated code. I followed the tutorial described here. BactDating v1.1.2 (Didelot et al. (2018)) BactDating is a Bayesian tool for dating ancestral nodes in bacterial phylogenetic trees, integrating molecular clock models with epidemiological or historical data. It’s particularly useful for reconstructing the evolutionary history of bacterial pathogens, estimating when key events (like outbreaks or divergences) occurred. Built in R, it uses a relaxed molecular clock and can incorporate uncertainty in tip dates (sampling times), making it flexible for messy real-world datasets. Nodes represent gene families (clusters of homologous genes across the input genomes). Edges connect gene families that are genomic neighbors (i.e., their sequences are adjacent in at least one genome). The graph is partitioned into categories—persistent, shell, and cloud—based on how frequently gene families appear across genomes and their neighborhood relationships. This structure resembles a “subway map” of genomic diversity, allowing you to visualize the core and variable components of a species’ pangenome. The ‘persistent,’ ‘shell,’ and ‘cloud’ genomes constitute 69.95%, 19.14%, and 10.91% of the pangenome, respectively (4.4). Figure 4.4: Pangenome graph of the 115 CA strains. ‘Persistent’: purple; ‘shell’: orange; ‘cloud’: green. 4.4.1.2 Copper Resistance-Related Genes Various copper resistance-related genes have been characterized in Xanthomonas and in Xaj. These genes include: copL, copA, copB, copC, copD, and copK (Lee et al. (1994); cesbron2015; Marin et al. (2019); Assis et al. (2021)). The copA and copC genes encode periplasmic copper-binding proteins, conferring partial copper resistance in P. syringae (Marin et al. (2019)). In X. citri, Richard et al. (2017) reported plasmid-bore copper resistance genes termed copABCD, however in Xaj these genes are found on the chromosome (Lee et al. (1994); Giovanardi et al. (2016); Assis et al. (2021)). In both copper-sensitive (CuS) and copper-resistant (CuR) Xanthomonas strains, the chromosomal genes cohL, cohA, and cohB, involved in copper homeostasis, exhibit homology to cop resistance genes located on plasmids (Franklin Behlau et al. (2011); F. Behlau, Fonseca, and Belasque Jr (2016)). The PPanGGoLiN analysis successfully identified copper resistance-related genes as well as the copper homeostatsis genes. The genes associated with copper resistance are copL family metal-binding regulatory protein, copper resistance system multicopper oxidase ( copA ), copper resistance protein B ( copB ), copper homeostasis periplasmic binding protein copC, copper homeostasis membrane protein copD, and copK family periplasmic copper-binding protein. Each of these six genes are present in the ‘shell’ or ‘cloud’ partitions and while the respective copL, copA, copB homeostasis genes are present in the ‘persistent’ genome and found in all 115 strains (4.4). Modules Definition: Modules in PPanGGOLiN are conserved groups of genes, typically from the variable (shell and cloud) genome, that tend to co-occur and are co-localized across multiple genomes in the pangenome. These are often hypothesized to represent functional units that are gained or lost together. How They’re Generated: Modules are predicted using the panModule method, which analyzes patterns of gene co-occurrence and genomic neighborhood within RGPs. The process involves identifying clusters of genes that consistently appear together in the variable regions of the pangenome. Spots Definition: Spots, or Spots of Insertion, are groups of RGPs from different genomes that share conserved flanking persistent genes, indicating a common insertion site in the pangenome. They represent hotspots of genomic variability. How They’re Generated: After RGPs are identified, the spot command groups them into Spots based on shared genomic context (persistent gene borders). This clustering reflects where RGPs tend to integrate across the pangenome. RGPs (Regions of Genomic Plasticity) Definition: RGPs are genomic regions in individual genomes that consist of genes from the shell and cloud partitions (i.e., non-persistent genes). These regions are typically associated with horizontal gene transfer (HGT) and often correspond to Genomic Islands (GIs). How They’re Generated: The panRGP method identifies RGPs by scanning each genome and detecting clusters of consecutive shell or cloud genes, using a score-based algorithm to define boundaries. Persistent genes flanking these regions help delineate them. Interconnection Modules, RGPs, and Spots are interconnected: Modules are often subsets of genes within RGPs, and Spots group RGPs across genomes. The –spot_modules option ties these together by associating Modules with specific Spots and RGPs, enabling a deeper understanding of how conserved gene clusters relate to variable genomic regions.
